stem: By how many prints does the median edition size increase when the eighth edition is included?
stimulus: A printmaking studio recorded the number of prints in each of its first 7 linocut editions: 18, 25, 12, 28, 20, 15, and 22. The studio then released an eighth edition of 140 prints and added it to the data.
explanation: Sort the original 7 values first: 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28. The median is the 4th value, 20. Add 140; it goes at the top of the list: 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 140. There are now 8 values, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values: (20 + 22)/2 = 21. The median rises by 21 − 20 = 1. The mean jumps from 140/7 = 20 to 280/8 = 35, a rise of 15. The extreme value pulls the mean hard toward it, but the median moves only half a position.

common_errors.why: Subtype trap: you assumed the median rises as much as the mean, and gave the mean's increase (from 20 to 35) instead.
You remembered that an outlier barely moves the median and decided it doesn't move at all. With 8 values, the median becomes the average of 20 and 22.
You found the new median but didn't subtract the original median of 20.
You gave the new mean of all 8 editions, not the change in the median.

stem: What is the median length, in minutes, of all 10 movements?
stimulus: A musicologist cataloguing a composer's suites listed the lengths, in minutes, of 9 movements: 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 9, 10, 11, and 13. A tenth movement was later discovered. When its length was added to the list, the mean length of the 10 movements was 10 minutes.
explanation: First find the missing length. The 9 listed lengths add up to 72. A mean of 10 for 10 movements means a total of 100, so the tenth movement is 100 − 72 = 28 minutes. That is longer than every other movement, so it goes at the end of the sorted list: 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 28. With 10 values, the median is the mean of the 5th and 6th values: (7 + 9)/2 = 8. The original median was 7, so the median moves only 1 while the mean moves 2.

common_errors.why: Subtype trap: the mean rose by 2 (from 8 to 10), and you assumed the median also rose by 2, from 7 to 9.
You assumed adding an extreme value leaves the median exactly where it was. With an even count, the median becomes the average of 7 and 9.
You stopped after finding the length of the tenth movement.
You gave the new mean, which the question already states, instead of the median.

stem: Of the mean numbers of meteors per hour at the three sites, what is the greatest?
stimulus:
During a meteor shower, observers at three sites counted meteors in a series of one-hour periods. The table shows how many hours at each site produced each count.

Number of Hours with Each Meteor Count
Meteors per hour | Site P | Site Q | Site R
10 | 1 | 4 | 1
20 | 3 | 2 | 1
30 | 5 | 1 | 2
40 | 3 | 2 | 3
50 | 1 | 4 | 3
explanation: Look for symmetry before you calculate. The frequencies for Site P (1, 3, 5, 3, 1) and for Site Q (4, 2, 1, 2, 4) are symmetric about 30, so each of those means is 30. Site R's frequencies are heavier at the high end, so its mean is above 30 and is the greatest. Compute it: 10(1) + 20(1) + 30(2) + 40(3) + 50(3) = 360 meteors over 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 10 hours, so the mean is 360/10 = 36. In Desmos: mean([10,20,30,40,50],[1,1,2,3,3]).

common_errors.why: You saw that the counts run from 10 to 50 and assumed every site centres on 30. That holds only for the symmetric tables, and you missed that Site R leans high.
You gave Site R's median (the 5th and 6th of its 10 sorted values are both 40) instead of its mean.
You divided Site R's total of 360 by the 5 rows of the table instead of by the 10 hours observed.
You stopped at Site R's total meteor count and didn't divide by the number of hours.

stem: By how many acres does the median park area decrease when the error is corrected?
stimulus: An urban planning office recorded the area, in acres, of the public parks in 8 neighborhoods: 18, 6, 120, 15, 23, 9, 20, and 14. An audit found that the value 120 was a typing error; that park's actual area is 12 acres.
explanation: Sort before you take any median. Original data: 6, 9, 14, 15, 18, 20, 23, 120. With 8 values, the median is (15 + 18)/2 = 16.5. Corrected data: 6, 9, 12, 14, 15, 18, 20, 23. The median is now (14 + 15)/2 = 14.5. The median decreases by 16.5 − 14.5 = 2. The corrected value moved from the top of the list to below the middle, so the middle pair shifts down one position. The mean falls by 108/8 = 13.5, far more than the median.

common_errors.why: Subtype trap: you assumed the median changes as much as the mean and gave the mean's decrease, 108/8.
You decided that fixing an outlier can't affect the median, or you took the 4th and 5th values from the unsorted list (15 and 23 both times), which gives no change.
You found the corrected median but didn't subtract it from the original median of 16.5.
You gave the change in the single corrected value (120 − 12), not the change in the median.
